msgs.title: Most traders spend the day staring at shadows on a wall.
msgs.pub:
Most traders spend the day staring at shadows on a wall.

In Plato's Republic, prisoners sit chained in a cave, facing the wall.

They see shadows of things carried behind them, and they take the shadows for the world.

The one-minute chart is our wall.

It flickers all day and tells you very little about what the business earns or who is selling size.

Some days the shadow matters. Price has the final word.

Even so, a prisoner who reads shadows faster stays a prisoner.

I look at the weekly chart before I touch anything.

Turn around once a day. The fire is behind you.

Every losing position gets the same promise: I will cut it, just not yet.

msgs.pub:
Your open profit is a rumor until you close the trade.

Herodotus tells how Croesus, the richest king of his day, asked Solon who was the happiest man alive.

Solon named men who were already dead. Call no one happy before the end, he said.

Croesus sent him away as a fool. Years later he lost his kingdom.

Traders send Solon away every bull market.

They screenshot the open gain and size the next trade off money they have not banked.

Then one gap down rewrites the whole year.

I do not know where this rally ends. Nobody does.

What I know is that a paper gain belongs to the market until I sell.

Count your gains the way Solon counted lives: at the end.

Dealers know where retail puts its stops.

Large holders know how long a small account can sit in a drawdown.

Someone always knows how much pain you can take. Make sure you know it first.
